chunks: The standing was appointed at al-Mashʿar and not within the Haram because the Kaʿbah is the House of Allah, the Haram is its veil, and al-Mashʿar is its door. When the visitors sought to approach it, He made them stand at the door, supplicating until He permitted them to enter. Then He made them stand at the second veil, which is Muzdalifah. When He saw the length of their supplication, He commanded them to draw near with their قربان. Then when they had offered, completed their untidiness-removal rites, and purified themselves from the sins that had been a veil for them before Him, He commanded them to visit in a state of purity.

key_terms.الْحَرَمِ: the sacred sanctuary around the Kaʿbah, described here as a veil
key_terms.الْمَشْعَرِ: al-Mashʿar, the sacred station presented here as the door of approach
key_terms.الْمَوْقِفُ: the appointed place of standing in the hajj rite
key_terms.تَفَثَهُمْ: their ritual untidiness or dishevelment removed upon completing rites
key_terms.حِجَابُهُ: its veil; a barrier or screen signifying graded access
key_terms.قُرْبَانِهِمْ: their sacrificial offering by which they draw near
key_terms.مُزْدَلِفَةُ: the hajj station identified here as the second veil

ai.seo_question: Why is the standing appointed at al-Mashʿar rather than inside the Haram in hajj?
ai.summary: This hadith explains the ritual stations of hajj through a symbolic theology of approach to Allah: the Kaʿbah as His House, the Haram as its veil, and al-Mashʿar as its door. It presents the pilgrim’s movement through supplication, sacrifice, and purification as a staged preparation for sacred visitation in a state of taharah.
